client: I've been really struggling with my new job at the startup. After missing that big deadline last week, I can't stop worrying that I'm not cut out for this role. The pressure just keeps building and I'm starting to doubt whether therapy can even help with work stress like this.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a heavy weight of self-doubt after that missed deadline, and that pressure is making you question both your abilities and whether therapy can help. Let's unpack that thought together - what makes you feel particularly "not cut out" for this role?

client: I just keep thinking about how my manager had to step in to finish my project. It makes me feel like I'm not competent enough for this job, even though I've been here for two years. Part of me wonders if therapy can really change the fact that I keep messing up at work.
therapist: That moment when your manager stepped in seems to have really shaken your confidence in your abilities, even with two years of experience behind you. I hear you questioning whether therapy can help with what feels like concrete work mistakes - would it help to explore how our thoughts about these situations might be influencing how we feel and perform?

client:
I get what you're saying about thoughts influencing feelings, but this wasn't just in my head - I actually messed up that client presentation. My manager had to step in and fix it in front of everyone. It's hard to just think my way out of that embarrassment when it was a real failure. 

I do want to feel more confident at work, but I'm not sure how therapy helps with actual job skills. Like what if I'm just not good enough at this role? That's what keeps going through my mind now.
therapist: I hear how painful that experience was, and you're absolutely right that the situation happened in reality - what we're working with here isn't just thoughts, but how those thoughts are impacting your ability to move forward. Would it help to explore how this one incident might be coloring how you view your overall competence?

client: I get what you're saying, but it's hard not to see this as proof that I'm just not good enough. That one mistake at work led to such big consequences - my boss still looks at me differently now. I keep replaying it in my head and thinking about all the ways I should have handled it better.
therapist: That moment clearly left a deep mark, and I can hear how it's become this defining proof of your abilities in your mind. When you say you keep replaying it, what do you notice happens to your confidence each time you revisit that memory?

client: Every time I replay that moment, I feel this sinking pit in my stomach, like I’m reliving the failure all over again. My confidence just crumbles—I start thinking, “See? You’re not capable. You’ll always mess up when it matters.” It’s like that memory just reinforces everything negative I already believe about myself. I know I shouldn’t dwell on it, but it feels impossible to let it go.
therapist: That sinking feeling and the way your mind keeps reinforcing those negative beliefs sounds incredibly painful to experience over and over. What do you think might happen if we gently examined that memory together, not to dismiss it, but to see if there might be other perspectives hidden in that moment?

client: I don't know... every time I try to think about that memory differently, it just makes me feel worse. Like I'm trying to trick myself into believing something that isn't true. The facts are what they are - I messed up and people got hurt because of me.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between the pain of the memory and the frustration of trying to change how you see it - that must feel exhausting. When you say "people got hurt," could we explore what exactly you mean by that, and whether the impact might have been different than what you're imagining?

client: I guess I mean that my actions directly caused pain to people I care about, and I can't stop replaying those moments in my head. But when you ask if the impact might be different than I imagine... that makes me uncomfortable because it feels like you're trying to minimize what happened. The guilt feels like proof that I deserve to feel this way.
therapist: I hear how deeply you're sitting with this guilt, and I want to honor that - this isn't about minimizing what happened, but about understanding whether the weight you're carrying matches the actual impact. When you say you "deserve" to feel this way, what does that belief do for you in your daily life?

client:
I don't know what that belief does for me... I guess it feels like some kind of punishment I have to endure. But when you ask it that way, it makes me realize how exhausting it is to carry this guilt around every single day. 

Part of me worries that if I stop feeling guilty, it means I don't care about what happened anymore. Like the guilt is the only thing proving I'm still a good person deep down.
therapist: It sounds like this guilt has become both a burden and a kind of moral compass for you - like letting it go might mean losing part of what makes you a caring person. What might it look like to honor what happened while also finding a way to carry that care forward without the constant self-punishment?

client:
That actually makes a lot of sense... but I'm scared that if I stop feeling guilty, it'll mean I don't care anymore. The guilt is what reminds me every day how badly I messed up. I just don't know how to separate caring from punishing myself - they feel like the same thing right now. 

It's like, if I'm not constantly beating myself up about it, doesn't that make me a worse person? Like I'm letting myself off too easy?
therapist: It sounds like guilt has become so intertwined with your sense of morality that letting go of one feels like risking the other - that's such an important insight to notice. What if we explored how you might keep your caring nature while finding a kinder way to hold yourself accountable - one that doesn't require constant suffering?

client:
I get what you're saying, but when I try to be kinder to myself, it just feels like I'm making excuses for my mistakes. The guilt is what keeps me from being selfish or careless again. Without it, how do I know I won't just repeat the same wrong things? 

It's like my guilt is this heavy weight I carry, but at least it proves I still care. If I put it down, who am I then?
therapist: It sounds like guilt has become a kind of proof of your moral compass, and letting it go feels risky - like you might lose your way without that weight to guide you. What if we explored how you might keep your caring nature while finding a gentler way to hold yourself accountable - one that doesn't require constant suffering?
